title: Date, text and title
short: Written about 1862 (Fr409, J303) in one of Dickinson's fascicles; first printed in 1890 under the editorial title 'Exclusion'.
body: The archive's text is the edited version of Poems (1890), where Todd and Higginson called the poem 'Exclusion' and adopted two of Dickinson's alternative readings in lines 3-4. Dickinson's fascicle text reads 'To her divine Majority - / Present no more -', with 'Obtrude' as an alternative, and offers 'Rush mat' and 'lids' as variants later. The poem is one of the touchstones of 1862, Dickinson's most productive year. Its subject, choosing one companion and closing the door on all others, has been read biographically, theologically and as an Emersonian poem of self-reliance.

title: the soul's choice
short: The soul chooses its company and then excludes the world; the verbs are decisive and final.
body: 'Society' means both companionship and the social world. The soul is feminine ('her'), sovereign and self-governing. Readers connect the poem with Emerson's self-reliance and inward retreat; Some readers hear Puritan theological language of election recast in Transcendentalist terms, so that the soul's choosing mimics God's choosing of the elect. Others read a personal choice of a single beloved, or the artist's choice of solitude.

title: shuts the door
short: The first of the poem's closing movements: after choosing, the soul shuts the door, as later the valves close.
body: The short second line enacts the shutting. Readers have heard biblical echoes: the parable of the wise virgins, after whom 'the door was shut' (Matthew 25:10), and the injunction to pray in the closet with the door shut (Matthew 6:6). The White Heat commentary notes that each stanza moves from long lines to short ones, a pattern of closing down that becomes sharper as the poem proceeds.

title: her divine majority
short: Several senses at once: the soul's chosen company, which is a 'majority' of one; its sovereign coming-of-age; and, possibly, the dead.
body: The word has puzzled readers. A 'majority' can be the larger number: the soul together with her chosen one, or with God, makes a majority against the world. It can also mean legal adulthood, so the soul has 'come of age' and governs herself (OED). A third, darker sense is 'the great majority', the dead (OED records 'to join the majority' for dying), which would make the chosen society otherworldly. 'Divine' may mean sacred or simply 'excellent'. The archive's 'On her' follows 1890; Dickinson wrote 'To her'.

title: Obtrude (manuscript 'Present')
short: Thrust yourself on her uninvited no longer; Dickinson's main reading was 'Present no more', with 'Obtrude' as a variant.
body: 'Obtrude' means to force oneself or something on another unasked (OED). It is the more aggressive alternative; 'Present' (offer, introduce, or present oneself at court) is cooler and more ceremonious. The 1890 editors chose 'Obtrude', the archive's reading. The command is addressed to the world at large, the would-be visitors of the next stanza. Its brusque imperative, after the stately first line, is the first sign of the poem's gradual hardening into the finality of 'stone'.

title: the chariot and the kneeling emperor
short: The greatest visitors, a chariot at the gate and an emperor on his knees, leave the soul 'Unmoved'.
body: The second stanza dramatises the refusal with royal images set against domestic humility: the chariot pauses at a 'low gate', the emperor kneels on her 'mat' (Dickinson's variant is 'Rush mat', a humble woven mat). The repetition of 'Unmoved' makes her indifference ceremonial. Critics note the inversion of hierarchy: power kneels to the private soul, not the soul to power.

title: an ample nation
short: Out of a whole populous people, the soul chooses only one.
body: 'Ample' (large, spacious) makes the choice drastic: a nation against a single person. The speaker steps back and speaks of the soul in the third person ('I've known her'), as if observing someone else; the White Heat commentary notes this distancing. The stanza moves from the plural world to 'one' and then to 'stone'. 'Nation' also gives the soul's choice a political scale, continuing the regal language of 'majority', chariot and emperor: the soul behaves like a sovereign state.

title: 'Choose one'
short: The two-syllable line is the poem's act of election, and its theological overtones are strong.
body: In Calvinist theology God chooses or 'elects' the saved, a doctrine still preached in Dickinson's Amherst. The soul's choosing mirrors that sovereign, inexplicable act, and the reading of the poem as Puritan language applied to Transcendentalist self-reliance turns on it. Whether the 'one' is a lover, a friend, God or the soul itself is left open.

sources.cite: Helen Vendler, Dickinson: Selected Poems and Commentaries (Harvard UP, 2010), commentary on F409

title: the valves of her attention
short: Attention shuts like a valve, or like the leaves of a folding door; Dickinson's variant was 'lids'.
body: 'Valve' had the older sense of one leaf of a double or folding door (OED, from Latin valva), which continues the door image of line 2, and also the anatomical sense of a valve of the heart or a shell's halves. The image is precise and chilling: attention is a mechanism that can be closed. Dickinson's alternative 'lids' would suggest eyelids or the lid of a coffin. The White Heat commentary reads the image as suggesting exclusion, blindness and suffocation.

title: 'Like stone': closure
short: The poem ends with two heavy stressed syllables; the rhyme 'one / stone' locks the chosen one inside the closure.
body: The stanzas shrink: each opens with long lines and ends with short ones, and the last lines of the third stanza are the shortest in the poem. The final 'Like stone' is two stresses in a row (a spondee), and critics hear it banging shut. The rhyme 'one / stone', exact to the eye but slant to the ear, encloses 'one' inside 'stone'. The image may recall the stone rolled before a tomb, consistent with a reading of the soul's society as death; the poem leaves the tone suspended between admiration and fear of such absolute choice.
